segments.text: I get very, very irritated with food that when you bite into it, it burns your mouth.
And then you have this thing you want to eat and you got to blow on it for like a few
seconds.
And fried chicken can be deceiving because on the outside, you might just tap it
with your finger and be like, all right, that's ready.
But it's trapping heat that could burn your tongue.
So I think it's important with a fried chicken sandwich.
You lock the temperature, texture, ratio, dialed in, or when you hand it to somebody at a
festival, they can eat it without fear of burning their tongue.
So I'm all about getting that texture on the outside, the moisture on the inside, and
they heat balanced, dialed in.
So I think when you get all those elements together, those are the main key factors I look
for in a fried chicken sandwich.
Hi, my name is James McDuffey.
The chef here at Joseph Leonard in the West Village.
What makes our fried chicken sandwich different?
It's a great question.
I think fried chicken is one of those things like a burger that is in its simplicity.
You can do it really, really well.
Or you can do it half-hazardly and it comes out not as amazing.
And I think ours is one of the better ones in the city.
Although there are some other fried chickens out there that I aspire to.
The chicken is brined, then marinated in Tabasco and buttermilk, then dredged in season flour,
and it's crisp, it's awesome.
I would go toe to toe with anybody out there on a fried chicken competition.
I want something that's going to bring some acid to my chicken sandwich.
I want something that's cold.
Like we use pickled cucumbers.
You know, I want something that's going to be cold.
It's going to bring nice acid.
It's going to balance the temperatures as well as the richness.
And you know, really, I think the right use of acid helps food it.
It's an exploding amount.
I think toppings make it unique.
I think just the way the chicken itself plays with the honey and the sweetness of that,
the spiciness in Tabasco, you know, the crunch of the cucumber and the radish in it.
I think it's a unique sandwich.
I think it's delicious.
And you know, it's one of those things we've tried taking it off the menu.
And we've had a lot of pushback from guests who come on a regular basis for it.
So we keep it around.
My philosophy on food, I think ultimately, no matter what, it boils down to one common
principle, which is the intention is to create a product that we're proud of that makes
the person eating it smile.
This is a damn good sandwich.
You know, we wanted to do what we call an American bistro here because we're in America,
I'm American, part of my family is American.
And then within that, you know, offer a few inflections of French food that we love.
We are trying really, really hard to make connections with our guests.
We are trying really, really hard to establish real, sincere, genuine, deep connections.
We're trying to make connections with the people that walk in our door.
And then if you're doing it well, then maybe that's unique.
